dimension: Routing and cascading among language models under cost and capability constraints
summary:
This is the densest, fastest-moving literature bearing on the question, and almost every component of the founder's proposal already exists in it as a named, published mechanism with measured results.

The cost-quality problem was formalised as a cascade in 2023 (FrugalGPT, arXiv:2305.05176), as a learned router in 2024 (RouteLLM, arXiv:2406.18665), and unified with proofs of optimality in 2025 (cascade routing, ICML PMLR v267 pp. 12987-13010). A 2026 TMLR survey (arXiv:2603.04445) catalogues 7 routing paradigms; a second survey (arXiv:2502.00409) catalogues timing, objective and implementation axes. The founder's cold-start probe is UniRoute (arXiv:2502.08773), which represents each model as a vector of per-cluster error rates on representative prompts and routes 30+ models never seen in training, and EmbedLLM (ICLR 2025, arXiv:2410.02223), which learns model embeddings from a sparse correctness matrix. The founder's recursive difficulty ladder is computerised adaptive testing under item response theory: tinyBenchmarks (ICML 2024, arXiv:2402.14992) estimates ability from 100 items within about 2% error; ATLAS (arXiv:2511.04689) matches whole-bank ability from 41 of 5,600 items; Fluid Benchmarking (arXiv:2509.11106) reports higher validity with 50 times fewer items. The founder's knockout tournament is dueling bandits, with a cost-aware best-arm-identification formulation accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (arXiv:2609.30360) and an earlier result (AAAI-22, Learning to Identify Top Elo Ratings) showing random and round-robin pairing are the sample-inefficient choices.

On the central hypothesis, the evidence is genuinely split. For domain-shaped capability: 60 models on 44 benchmarks factor into 8 skills, and 2 models 6 Elo points apart have visibly different skill profiles (arXiv:2507.20208). Models of comparable accuracy disagree on 16% to 66% of items (arXiv:2602.11898). Per-item oracles beat the best single model by 12.0 points on one benchmark (arXiv:2606.27288) and up to 27.8 points under tight budgets (arXiv:2608.12150). Against it: an exploratory factor analysis of 156 models on 10 benchmarks found a single factor explaining 75% of total variance (arXiv:2603.02540), and realised gains from exploiting heterogeneity are small — 0.80 percentage points over quality-only team selection (arXiv:2609.38274).

mechanisms.name: FrugalGPT LLM cascade
mechanisms.what_it_does: Sends each query to a chain of models ordered cheapest-first; a learned scoring function judges whether the current answer is reliable and otherwise escalates. An optimiser picks the model ordering and per-stage thresholds to maximise expected accuracy under an average-cost budget, with cascades capped at length 3.
mechanisms.citation: Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou, "FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance", arXiv:2305.05176 (May 2023), later TMLR 2024. Code: github.com/stanford-futuredata/FrugalGPT
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It does not. The scoring function is trained offline on labelled examples, and the cascade order is fitted before deployment. Cold start is assumed away by the existence of a labelled training set.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Price heterogeneity is the paper's entire premise: it reports API fees differing by 2 orders of magnitude. Participant heterogeneity (desktop vs supercomputer) is handled only as a scalar per-call cost.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The tiering idea transfers directly and is the thing being rediscovered. What breaks if adopted naively: the cap of 3 is not arbitrary. FrugalGPT's cascade is a fixed global order, not a per-claim ranking, so it cannot express the founder's positional hypothesis at all. CDSFL would need the per-query variant (RouteLLM or cascade routing), not this one.

mechanisms.name: Cascade depth is almost never worth more than 2
mechanisms.what_it_does: Gives first-order optimality conditions for when a deferral boundary in a cascade pays for itself: at the optimum, the ratio of expected accuracy gain to expected downstream cost is equal across boundaries. Decomposes the advantage of score-based over random escalation into 2 AUROC terms.
mechanisms.citation: Dylan Bouchard, "Is Escalation Worth It? On the Depth of LLM Cascades", arXiv:2605.06350v2 (2026)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not addressed. It assumes a pool of 8 models with measured per-benchmark accuracy and 9 candidate deferral scores already in hand.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Only as cost in the optimality condition. The analysis is cost-aware but participant-agnostic.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the sharpest measured objection to the founder's recursive tier ladder. Two-model cascades beat single-model selection by 2.1 to 8.2 percentage points across 5 benchmarks. Going beyond 2 models did not improve mean test accuracy in 118 of 135 comparisons, adding at most 0.43 percentage points. Deeper cascades helped only when the confidence score discriminated the CURRENT model's correct from incorrect answers, and the gain vanished when the score instead reflected query difficulty shared across models. A falsification harness's natural score — how hard this claim is — is exactly the shared-difficulty kind that was measured to kill the benefit. If CDSFL builds a 4-tier or 5-tier ladder, this paper predicts tiers 3 and up contribute under half a percentage point.

mechanisms.name: RouteLLM: router learned from preference data, transferable across model pairs
mechanisms.what_it_does: Trains a binary router from pairwise human preference votes to predict whether a strong model will beat a weak one on a given prompt, then routes to hit a target such as 90% of the strong model's quality at minimum cost. Uses data augmentation for out-of-domain robustness.
mechanisms.citation: Isaac Ong et al., "RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data", arXiv:2406.18665; ICLR 2025 as "Learning to Route LLMs from Preference Data". Blog: lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm/
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By importing a prior: the training signal is Chatbot Arena preference votes, and model tiers are formed by clustering leaderboard position. This is precisely the vendor-reputation prior the founder's constraints forbid.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Reduces the roster to 2 tiers (strong/weak). It does not scale structurally to 70 or 700 participants without redesign, which is the founder's explicit constraint.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: One result transfers and matters: the routers kept their performance when the strong and weak models were swapped at test time. That is evidence the routing signal is a property of the QUERY, not of the model identities, which supports CDSFL's measured-capability rule. What breaks: the 2-tier formulation, and the leaderboard-derived tiering, both of which violate stated constraints and must be replaced.

mechanisms.name: UniRoute: per-cluster error vectors for models never seen in training
mechanisms.what_it_does: Represents each model as a K-dimensional vector of its error rates on K prompt clusters (found by K-means on a training set). For a new prompt, routes to the model with the lowest cost-adjusted error in that prompt's cluster. A model that joins later is described by running it on the representative prompts; no router retraining. Proves both instantiations estimate a theoretically optimal routing rule, with an excess risk bound.
mechanisms.citation: Wittawat Jitkrittum et al., "Universal Model Routing for Efficient LLM Inference", arXiv:2502.08773 (Feb 2025); workshop version "Universal LLM Routing with Correctness-Based Representation", ICLR 2025 workshop
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: This IS the founder's cold-start mechanism, formalised and with a risk bound. A new model is probed on representative prompts and its error vector placed in the same space as the incumbents. Experiments route among more than 30 unseen models.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Cost enters the routing rule as a cost-adjusted error, so a cheap-and-adequate participant can win a cluster it is good at. Cluster structure is what makes the representation domain-shaped rather than scalar.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers almost without modification, and is the single closest published match to the founder's proposal. The founder's "hard random maths problem" is UniRoute's representative-prompt set with K=1; the recursion into easier problems is K>1 with difficulty-stratified clusters. What breaks if adopted: UniRoute's clusters come from K-means on prompt embeddings, which for CDSFL would cluster claims by surface text rather than by falsification difficulty. CDSFL would have to define its own cluster axis (claim type, tool requirement, severity class) and would then inherit the excess risk bound only if the clusters are fixed before probing.

mechanisms.name: EmbedLLM: model embeddings learned from a sparse correctness matrix
mechanisms.what_it_does: An encoder-decoder learns a compact vector per model by reconstructing whether that model answers each question correctly. One embedding then serves correctness forecasting, routing, and benchmark-accuracy prediction without extra inference. Probing shows the embeddings capture traits such as code specialisation without being trained for it.
mechanisms.citation: Richard Zhuang, Tianhao Wu, Zhaojin Wen, Andrew Li, Jiantao Jiao, Kannan Ramchandran, "EmbedLLM: Learning Compact Representations of Large Language Models", arXiv:2410.02223; ICLR 2025
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: A new model needs only a partial row of the correctness matrix, because the decoder fills the rest. This is strictly cheaper than the founder's exhaustive probe: it does not require every model to attempt every probe problem.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: The embedding is a vector, so a participant can be strong on one axis and weak on another. Heterogeneous compute is not modelled; only measured correctness is.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and answers the 700-model scaling constraint: the correctness matrix is sparse by design, so the probe cost grows sub-quadratically. What breaks: the embedder itself must be trained on a reasonably dense initial matrix, so the very first cold start still requires a seed of probed models. CDSFL would need a seeding policy, and the paper does not give one.

mechanisms.name: Zooter: reward-distilled routing, and the measurement that expertise is per-task
mechanisms.what_it_does: Distils a reward model's normalised scores on training queries into a lightweight routing function, so inference activates 1 model plus a small router instead of generating from all candidates. Tag-wise rewards combined linearly mitigate reward-model noise.
mechanisms.citation: Lu et al., "Routing to the Expert: Efficient Reward-guided Ensemble of Large Language Models", arXiv:2311.08692; NAACL 2024 (aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.109)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Poorly, and the surveys say so: training relies on a fixed set of models, so adaptability to new or unseen models is limited. The founder's roster-growth constraint breaks it.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Outputs a categorical distribution over the pool, so it is per-task rather than scalar, which is the right shape. It does not model compute asymmetry.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The method does not transfer (fixed roster), but one measurement is the most citable piece of evidence for the positional hypothesis in the routing literature: evaluated on a collection of 26 subsets across different domains and tasks, Zooter outperformed the best single model on average and ranked first on 44% of tasks. A router that is best on 44% of tasks is only possible if capability is domain-shaped. Also a caution: on the hardest benchmark it scored 32.3 against 88.3 for the strongest single model, so per-domain routing can route confidently into a tier that simply cannot do the task.

mechanisms.name: RouterBench and the oracle ceiling
mechanisms.what_it_does: Provides 405,000+ precomputed inference outcomes from 11 models over commonsense reasoning, QA, conversation, maths, coding and retrieval-augmented generation, so routers can be trained and compared without paying for inference. Defines the Oracle router: always route to the best-performing model, breaking ties by cheapest.
mechanisms.citation: Qitian Jason Hu et al., "RouterBench: A Benchmark for Multi-LLM Routing System", arXiv:2403.12031. Code: github.com/withmartian/routerbench
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a cold-start method, but it is the correct instrument for measuring one: a cold-start policy can be replayed against the precomputed matrix at zero inference cost.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Cost is a first-class axis; the Oracle's tie-break is cheapest-wins.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The method CDSFL should copy is the Oracle baseline, not any particular router. The Oracle's selection frequencies are the measurement: 2 models with roughly 50% accuracy across tasks were selected often because they were cheap and correct when it counted, while the most capable model was seldom chosen. That is the founder's thesis, measured. What breaks: the Oracle is a ceiling, not a deployable policy, and CDSFL must report the gap between its router and the Oracle rather than the router's raw score.

mechanisms.name: Routing collapse (degenerate convergence) and the objective-decision mismatch
mechanisms.what_it_does: Documents that as the cost budget rises, existing routers systematically default to the most capable and most expensive model even when a cheaper one suffices. Attributes it to training routers to predict scalar performance scores when routing actually depends on discrete comparisons, so small prediction errors flip model orderings. Proposes EquiRouter, which learns rankings directly.
mechanisms.citation: Guannan Lai, Han-Jia Ye, "When Routing Collapses: On the Degenerate Convergence of LLM Routers", arXiv:2602.03478 (Feb 2026)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not addressed.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Directly: collapse is the failure to use small participants, which is exactly the founder's "no model is ever permanently set aside" concern expressed as a measured defect.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is a measured instance of the founder's own worry, and it names the cause. If CDSFL ranks seats by predicting a scalar capability score, the prediction error will flip orderings and the system will collapse onto the strongest seat, silently retiring the rest in practice while the policy nominally keeps them. The fix in the paper is to learn the RANKING, not the score, which is architecturally the founder's tournament rather than his probe. EquiRouter reduced cost by about 17% at the strongest-model performance level on RouterBench. CDSFL should instrument per-seat selection frequency and treat a seat falling to near-zero traffic as a defect, not an outcome.

mechanisms.name: When is Routing Meaningful: diversity saturates, and accuracy is not meaningfulness
mechanisms.what_it_does: Argues routing needs 2 properties beyond accuracy and cost: the pool must be behaviourally varied (identical actors make routing pointless), and the policy must be consistent (rewordings of one query go to the same actor). Adapts Hierarchic Social Entropy to measure pool diversity and adds a perturbation-based robustness metric.
mechanisms.citation: Fantine Huot, Michael Kaisers, Mirella Lapata, "When is Routing Meaningful? Diversity and Robustness in Language Model Societies", arXiv:2607.09197 (2026)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not directly, but it bounds the problem: if fewer than 10 well-chosen agents capture most of the available diversity in a large pool, the cold-start probe does not need to rank all 700 participants to capture the routable signal.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Heterogeneity is the object of measurement. The finding is strongly diminishing returns in it.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Two things transfer. First, the saturation result directly attacks the premise that a 700-model roster needs full ranking: fewer than 10 well-chosen agents captured most available diversity. Second, the consistency requirement is a falsifiable test CDSFL can run cheaply — reword a claim and check the seat assignment is unchanged. The paper's own summary is the warning: accuracy and meaningfulness can sharply diverge, and a router can score well on accuracy while failing both properties. Also relevant: nearest-neighbour routers became more accurate with specialist pools but lost robustness under perturbation, while prompted routing stayed stable.

mechanisms.name: Bandit routing and the measured cold-start collapse
mechanisms.what_it_does: Treats routing as a contextual bandit learned from reward feedback instead of a labelled routing set. Hybrid designs fit an offline prior from a curated probe set (a full reward matrix over candidate models), then continue learning online from bandit feedback on the selected arm only.
mechanisms.citation: Reward Model Routing in Alignment, arXiv:2510.02850; OrcaRouter, "A Production-Oriented LLM Router with Hybrid Offline-Online Learning", arXiv:2605.30736; LLM Bandit, arXiv:2502.02743
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: This literature is the direct answer to the founder's question and it reports a specific failure: LinUCB often collapses to a single fixed arm after a few batches, likely because per-arm observations are scarce and contexts are similar, leading to premature exploitation. The fix adopted was Bayesian Thompson sampling to keep exploring. The stated trade-off is that an offline router has abundant data but degrades under distribution shift, while a pure online router adapts but suffers cold start and exploration problems.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Per-arm models with a cost-aware reward; a cheap arm can win on reward-per-unit-cost.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Transfers directly and supplies the missing half of the founder's design. His probe is OrcaRouter's offline warmup — evaluate each candidate on a curated set of routing prompts to get a reward matrix. What he has not specified is the online half, and without it the measured outcome is arm collapse: the same defect as routing collapse above, arriving by a different route. CDSFL needs a forced-exploration floor and per-seat pull counts monitored, or the cold-start ranking freezes and stops tracking real capability drift.

mechanisms.name: Cost-aware best-arm identification with dueling feedback
mechanisms.what_it_does: A multi-armed bandit variant with 2 features matching the founder's tournament exactly: dueling feedback, where pairwise comparisons between model responses are the only signal, and heterogeneous sampling costs, because querying different models costs differently. Assumes a Condorcet winner exists (validated empirically on several real datasets) and proposes a Track-and-Stop algorithm for best-arm identification at prescribed confidence, proven to achieve asymptotically optimal cost.
mechanisms.citation: Sarvesh Gharat, Nikhil Karamchandani, Jayakrishnan Nair, "Cost-Aware Best-LLM Identification using Dueling Feedback", arXiv:2609.30360 (24 Sep 2026), accepted at NeurIPS 2026
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is a pure cold-start method: no prior over arms is assumed, only pairwise outcomes. This is the founder's "names drawn from a bag", formalised, with an optimality guarantee the bag-draw does not have.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Heterogeneous per-arm query cost is built into the sampling rule, and it reports consistent improvements over cost-unaware algorithms and their cost-aware extensions.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the second mechanism the founder has reinvented, and the published version is strictly better than a knockout bracket: it allocates comparisons adaptively rather than by bracket position, and it stops at a stated confidence rather than when the bracket runs out. The load-bearing assumption to check is the Condorcet winner — some participant that beats every other in pairwise comparison. If CDSFL's seats are genuinely domain-shaped, no Condorcet winner exists globally, only per-domain, and the guarantee applies per cluster rather than over the whole roster.

mechanisms.name: Dueling bandits for top-rating identification: random and round-robin pairing are the inefficient choices
mechanisms.what_it_does: Maintains a candidate set of promising players, selects pairs by an upper-confidence-bound rule, and updates Elo-style ratings, in order to identify the top-rated player with far fewer comparisons than uniform or round-robin schemes.
mechanisms.citation: Learning to Identify Top Elo Ratings: A Dueling Bandits Approach, AAAI-22 (ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/20860). Background: Busa-Fekete, Hullermeier, El Mesaoudi-Paul, "Preference-based Online Learning with Dueling Bandits: A Survey", JMLR 22 (18-546)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: By design: it starts with no prior and concentrates comparisons where the uncertainty is.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not cost-aware; that extension is the NeurIPS 2026 paper above.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the direct refutation of the second mechanism as stated. Pairing "as names drawn from a bag" is uniform sampling, and the published finding is that uniform and round-robin pairing are the sample-inefficient baselines. A knockout bracket is worse still, because it spends comparisons on pairs whose outcome is already near-certain and eliminates participants after a single result — which also violates the founder's own constraint that no participant is permanently set aside. Replace random pairing with upper-confidence-bound pair selection and the mechanism becomes defensible.

mechanisms.name: Chatbot Arena: Bradley-Terry with active (non-uniform) pair sampling
mechanisms.what_it_does: Collects pairwise human votes, fits a Bradley-Terry model for ratings with confidence intervals, and chooses which pair to show non-uniformly — in proportion to the reduction in confidence-interval size that sampling that pair would produce, concentrating votes on pairs of similar strength where uncertainty is highest.
mechanisms.citation: Wei-Lin Chiang et al., "Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference", arXiv:2403.04132; ICML 2024. Active-sampling evaluation used a 213,576-point holdout set.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: New entrants are sampled preferentially, which is the standard answer to a cold roster. Note the measured deviation: deployed sampling rates were reported as often inconsistent with the stated policy.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not at all. A rating is a scalar, and cost and compute are outside the model.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The estimation machinery transfers; the scalar output does not. Bradley-Terry with confidence intervals is the right way to turn CDSFL's pairwise falsification outcomes into rankings, and active pair selection is the right way to spend a comparison budget. But fitting 1 Bradley-Terry parameter per seat is exactly the scalar capability the founder's positional hypothesis rejects. CDSFL should fit per-cluster Bradley-Terry models, which is what the non-transitivity literature below independently recommends.

mechanisms.name: Elo is order-sensitive and hyperparameter-sensitive
mechanisms.what_it_does: Tests whether Elo satisfies 2 properties a robust evaluation needs: reliability (invariance to incidental choices such as match order and the K-factor) and transitivity. Finds that from a single sequence of matches, scores can fluctuate dramatically based solely on the arbitrary ordering of matches when win probabilities approach 0.5, and that ratings stabilise only with 100 or more comparison permutations.
mechanisms.citation: Meriem Boubdir et al., "Elo Uncovered: Robustness and Best Practices in Language Model Evaluation", arXiv:2311.17295; GEM workshop 2023 (aclanthology.org/2023.gem-1.28), pp. 339-352; NeurIPS 2024 poster
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is a critique of the cold-start mechanism the founder proposes. Online Elo is most unstable exactly where the founder's tournament spends most of its matches: between closely matched participants.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not addressed.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the most direct published reason the knockout tournament will not produce a stable ranking. A bracket is 1 ordering of matches. The paper's own remedy — average over 100+ permutations — costs 100 times the bracket, and the slides note comparison count grows quadratically. The practical consequence for CDSFL: a bracket result is not a measurement, it is 1 draw from a distribution, and the founder's own measured-capability constraint therefore forbids acting on a single bracket. Use batch Bradley-Terry with intervals instead of sequential Elo.

mechanisms.name: Non-transitivity in LLM-as-judge: brackets assume what the judges do not deliver
mechanisms.what_it_does: Shows that judge preferences are non-transitive, so rankings built from comparison against a fixed baseline are sensitive to the choice of baseline. Introduces Soft Non-Transitivity Deviation, comparing observed pairwise win rates against those a Bradley-Terry fit predicts under transitivity. Recommends full round-robin plus Bradley-Terry instead.
mechanisms.citation: Yi Xu et al., "Investigating Non-Transitivity in LLM-as-a-Judge", arXiv:2502.14074; ICML 2025 spotlight. Related: TrustJudge, arXiv:2509.21117, reports pairwise transitivity inconsistency of 15.22% with one 70B-class judge, reduced to 4.40%. ELSPR, arXiv:2505.17691, detects cycles in tournament graphs and reports non-transitivity reduced by 13.78% after training-data purification.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a cold-start method; it is a precondition check on any tournament.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Reports that cycles concentrate in near-equal pairs, where the quality difference falls below the just noticeable difference, and that non-transitive pairs show higher textual similarity.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: A single-elimination bracket is only valid if preference is transitive, and the measured violation rate on a strong judge was 15.22% of comparisons. In a 700-participant bracket, roughly 699 matches decide the ranking, and a 15% per-match error that is not independent of pair closeness will not average out — it will systematically mis-seed the upper rounds. The published fix is round-robin plus Bradley-Terry, which is quadratic, so CDSFL must choose: pay the quadratic cost, use the adaptive dueling-bandit sampler, or accept an unquantified ranking. There is no cheap transitive bracket.

mechanisms.name: LLM-as-judge biases, including family-conditioned preference in panels
mechanisms.what_it_does: Measures position, verbosity and self-preference bias in judges, and — in the panel setting that matches CDSFL — measures whether a judge favours candidates from its own model family, using an estimator that holds candidate family fixed.
mechanisms.citation: Lianmin Zheng et al., "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena", arXiv:2306.05685, NeurIPS 2023: only the strongest judge gave consistent verdicts in more than 60% of cases when answer order was swapped. Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge, arXiv:2410.21819: highest self-preference score of 8 models tested was 0.520. David Ababio Awuni et al., "Who Judges Matters: Measuring Family-Conditioned Preference in LLM-as-Judge Panels", arXiv:2609.17857: 4 open-weight families, fully crossed, 9,312 judgments.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a cold-start method. It is the reason a cold-start tournament judged by the participants themselves does not measure capability.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Measures bias conditional on model family, which is the closest published analogue of CDSFL's multi-seat panel.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the hardest constraint on both of the founder's mechanisms, because both need a judge. The panel paper reports a same-family lift of 3.4 to 8.4 percentage points in all 4 families, a global family-preference statistic of 0.067 (95% CI 0.053 to 0.084, permutation p = 0.0002), 55.4% of AB/BA pairs reversing under order swap, and — decisively for CDSFL — panel composition changing 18.5% of pairwise outcomes relative to a family-balanced reference. If CDSFL's seats judge each other's falsifications, the measured ranking is partly a function of which families are seated. The founder's constraint that capability is measured, never a vendor name, is violated from the inside: the vendor name re-enters through the judge. Mitigations with published support: swap-order both ways and report flip rate, enforce family balance in the panel, and prefer reference-based grading over reference-free.

mechanisms.name: Verifiable grading of mathematical proofs is substantially weaker than final-answer checking
mechanisms.what_it_does: Measures the gap between a correct final answer and a sound proof, and the gap between what human experts and LLM judges score.
mechanisms.citation: Open Proof Corpus, arXiv:2506.21621: requiring proof correctness cost one strong model 8% of its final-answer accuracy and another nearly 30%. IneqMath, "Solving Inequality Proofs with Large Language Models", arXiv:2506.07927: once step-wise judges inspect every reasoning step, overall accuracy plummets by up to 65.5%, with judge F1 above 0.9 on a hand-labelled development set. QEDBench, arXiv:2602.20629: a frontier judge inflated scores by up to +0.18 mean score delta in abstract domains. LiveBench, arXiv:2406.19314: a judge given ground truth can verify answers, but a reference-free judge on competition maths had high error rates.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It is the strongest available support for the SHAPE of the founder's probe and the strongest caution about its SCORING.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Not addressed.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The founder chose well: a randomly generated maths problem with a checkable answer is one of the few probes where grading does not route through a biased judge, which sidesteps the family-preference problem above. But his criterion is not just the answer — it is "writing proofs and falsifiers to validate or disprove the result". That is precisely the part the measurements say cannot be graded reliably: up to 65.5% accuracy collapse under step-wise scrutiny, and judge leniency on fluent but wrong proofs. The split CDSFL should make: score the ANSWER mechanically (reliable, cheap, contamination-resistant if generated fresh), and treat proof quality as a separate, reference-based, marking-scheme-guided measurement with its own reported agreement rate — never as an undifferentiated component of a single "top performer" score.

mechanisms.name: Item response theory and computerised adaptive testing: the founder's difficulty ladder, already built
mechanisms.what_it_does: Models each item by difficulty and discrimination and each model by a latent ability, then selects the next item that maximises Fisher information about that model's ability — which in practice means harder items for stronger models and easier ones for weaker, recursing until the ability estimate is confident. Exactly the founder's recursion.
mechanisms.citation: Felipe Maia Polo et al., "tinyBenchmarks: evaluating LLMs with fewer examples", arXiv:2402.14992, ICML 2024: 100 curated examples per scenario estimate performance within about 2% error on average, versus 14,000 examples for the full MMLU. ATLAS, "Adaptive Testing for LLM Evaluation: A Psychometric Alternative to Static Benchmarks", arXiv:2511.04689: reduces required items by up to 90%, matching whole-bank ability with 41 items of 5,600 (0.157 MAE), and finds 3% to 6% of items have negative discrimination, indicating annotation errors. Fluid Language Model Benchmarking, arXiv:2509.11106 (AI2): higher validity and less variance on MMLU with 50 times fewer items.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Directly and optimally. Adaptive item selection IS the mechanism for ranking an unknown test-taker in the fewest trials, and the information-theoretic selection rule is the published improvement over the founder's heuristic of "hard problem first, then easier for the losers".
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Ability is estimated on a latent scale that is comparable across test-takers who saw different items — which is exactly what the founder needs when a desktop participant and a server participant cannot be given the same workload. Multidimensional IRT (arXiv:2610.05613) models a general trait plus domain-specific competencies hierarchically, borrowing information across domains for better per-domain scores.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the third mechanism already invented, and it is the one with the longest pedigree (adaptive testing predates all of this literature by decades). It transfers directly. The one thing that breaks: adaptive testing requires a pre-calibrated item bank — item difficulties and discriminations estimated from many prior test-takers. The founder's problems are "randomly generated", so they are uncalibrated by construction, and an uncalibrated item gives an unusable ability estimate. CDSFL must either calibrate a bank first (which costs the dense probing the founder wanted to avoid) or use a generator whose difficulty parameter is known analytically. The negative-discrimination finding is a bonus: 3% to 6% of items in a mature bank are broken, so a random generator will produce broken probes too and needs a discard rule.

mechanisms.name: Benchmark contamination: measured capability drifts because the probe leaks
mechanisms.what_it_does: Builds a fresh test set matched in style and difficulty to an existing one and measures the gap, as a test for overfitting to the public benchmark.
mechanisms.citation: Hugh Zhang et al., "A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic" (GSM1k), arXiv:2405.00332: 1,205 fresh grade-school problems; accuracy drops of up to 8%, with several model families showing systematic overfitting, while others showed little or none; Spearman r^2 = 0.36 between a model's probability of generating a GSM8K example and its performance gap. Questionable practices in machine learning, arXiv:2407.12220: models whose launch reports did not mention contamination dropped around 10%, others under 3%, and results were sensitive to prompt choice. LessLeak-Bench, arXiv:2502.06215, across 83 software-engineering benchmarks.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: It justifies the founder's choice of RANDOMLY GENERATED problems over a fixed benchmark, which is the correct defence.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Contamination is uneven across participants (up to 8% for some families, near 0 for others), so a fixed probe set does not just add noise, it adds a per-participant bias.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Vindicates one design choice and constrains another. Randomly generated probes are contamination-resistant, so the founder is right to prefer them. But the GSM1k authors' own caveat applies to him: a gap on a matched fresh set is also consistent with imperfect matching, with the fresh set being harder along an unmatched dimension. CDSFL cannot claim its random generator produces difficulty-matched problems without measuring that, and an unmatched generator makes tier assignments a function of which draw a participant got. A measured rate is needed: generate n problems, check the spread of outcomes across a fixed reference set of participants, and report it.

mechanisms.name: Budget-dependent rankings: there is no single ordering of participants
mechanisms.what_it_does: Varies the token generation budget across 7 levels from 64 to 4,096 and re-measures rankings, over 4 models on 3 reasoning benchmarks, 56,476 inferences.
mechanisms.citation: Rodrigo Guedes de Souza, Alison R. Panisson, "Who Thinks Best Depends on How Long You Let Them: Budget-Dependent Rankings in LLM Evaluation", arXiv:2608.12150 (Aug 2026)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a cold-start method, but it falsifies the output format the founder's cold start produces.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Budget IS the heterogeneity axis the founder cares about: a desktop participant is a low-budget participant. The paper measures what happens to rankings when budget varies, which is the desktop-versus-supercomputer question in its measurable form.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The headline finding is that model rankings reverse across budgets on all benchmarks (p < 0.01, McNemar). A single ranked roster is therefore not a well-defined object; the ranking is a function of the budget at which it was measured. Also: 3% to 19% of items get LESS accurate with more budget, model-specific, with only 6% to 14% cross-model overlap — so "solved fastest" and "solved correctly" are not the same ordering, and the founder's composite "fastest and most cost-effective" criterion silently fixes a budget. The complementarity number is the largest in this literature: a per-item oracle gains up to +27.8 percentage points, most at constrained budgets. And the caution: a budget-feature router captured 14.1% of that oracle gap cross-domain, gaining +1.6 to +5.7 points within a domain but LOSING 1.2 points on transfer to other domains. Domain-shaped routing learned in one domain actively hurts in another.

mechanisms.name: Low-rank skill factors: the strongest measurement that capability is a vector
mechanisms.what_it_does: Factor-analyses a 60-model by 44-benchmark performance matrix (24 model families) into latent skills, choosing factor count by Kaiser's rule and an 85% cumulative-variance threshold.
mechanisms.citation: Aviya Maimon, Amir David Nisan Cohen, Gal Vishne, Shauli Ravfogel, Reut Tsarfaty, "From Benchmarks to Skills: Low-Rank Factors for LLM Evaluation", arXiv:2507.20208v2
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: A new participant's skill profile is its loadings on 8 established factors, estimable from a subset of benchmarks — which is the founder's probe, with the probe axes derived rather than guessed.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: 8 factors: General NLU; Fine-Grained Entailment and Token Bias; Document Reading, Retrieval and Summarization; Truthful Instruction Generation; Specialized Domain-Knowledge QA; Social/Ethical Judgment; Faithful Summarization and Quantitative Precision; Grad-Level Scientific and Legal Reasoning. Every task's uniqueness is below about 0.40 (maximum 0.38), and internal consistency is Cronbach alpha 0.836, McDonald omega 0.821.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the evidence FOR the positional hypothesis, and it is the best-measured instance of it. The decisive observation: 2 models with nearly identical arena ratings (1322 and 1316) have clearly different skill profiles. That is a direct demonstration that a scalar ranking discards routable information. What transfers: the method, which CDSFL can run on its own seat-by-task outcome matrix to DERIVE its positions rather than assert them. What breaks: 8 factors were found over general NLP benchmarks, not over falsification tasks, so CDSFL cannot borrow these 8 axes — it must factor its own matrix, and that needs a reasonably dense matrix first.

mechanisms.name: A single general factor explaining 75% of variance: the strongest measurement AGAINST
mechanisms.what_it_does: Runs exploratory factor analysis on 156 models across 10 benchmarks (reasoning, code, long context, competition maths, verifiable instruction following, terminal use, multi-task knowledge, agentic tool use, and a hard general exam). Parallel analysis indicated a single-factor solution, and that factor accounted for 75% of the total variance.
mechanisms.citation: A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities, arXiv:2603.02540v2 (2026), factor analysis in Table 3
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: If one factor carries 75% of variance, a cold start needs to estimate essentially 1 number, which makes the founder's single hard problem a defensible probe and makes the recursion largely redundant.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: It denies that much heterogeneity exists on these benchmarks. The residual 25% is where any positional advantage must live.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the paper to put in front of the founder, because it is the cleanest refutation of the strong form of his hypothesis. 156 models, 10 benchmarks, 1 factor, 75% of variance. A football-position analogy requires positions to be largely orthogonal; 75% shared variance says they are mostly the same axis. The honest reading, reconciling it with the 8-factor result: the benchmark set determines the answer. The single-factor study used frontier "intelligence" benchmarks that are correlated by construction; the 8-factor study used 44 heterogeneous NLP tasks. For CDSFL the question is empirical and local — factor its OWN seat-by-claim matrix and report the variance share of the first component. If it is near 75%, the positional architecture is not worth its complexity and a cost-ordered cascade of depth 2 is the right design.

mechanisms.name: Benchmark Illusion: equal scores, different question-level profiles
mechanisms.what_it_does: Measures item-level disagreement between models of comparable aggregate accuracy on 2 reasoning benchmarks, then re-analyses published studies that used models as annotators.
mechanisms.citation: Eddie Yang, Dashun Wang, "Benchmark Illusion: Disagreement among LLMs and Its Scientific Consequences", arXiv:2602.11898 (Feb 2026), MMLU-Pro and GPQA
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not a cold-start method, but it quantifies how much information a single aggregate probe score throws away.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Models with comparable accuracy disagree on 16% to 66% of items; among top-performing frontier models the range is 16% to 38%.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This is the measurement that reconciles the 2 factor-analysis results and supports the founder's intuition in its WEAK form. Aggregate capability can be near-identical while per-item behaviour differs on up to 38% of items even among the strongest participants. So a scalar ranking is not wrong about aggregate ability; it is blind to which items each participant gets wrong — and a falsification harness cares only about the latter. The downstream finding matters for CDSFL's own validity: switching the annotation model changed estimated treatment effects by more than 80% and in some cases reversed their sign. Any CDSFL rate that depends on which seat was assigned is exposed to the same instability, which is an argument for recording seat assignment alongside every measured rate.

mechanisms.name: Measured complementarity ceilings, and how little of them is realisable
mechanisms.what_it_does: Measures the oracle ceiling (items solved by at least 1 participant) against the best single participant, and the error correlation that determines how much of the gap aggregation can recover.
mechanisms.citation: When Does Combining Language Models Help?, arXiv:2606.27288: best single model 0.850 on MMLU-Pro versus per-query oracle 0.970, a gain of 0.120, shrinking to 0.044 on a saturated multi-domain mix; on one hard science benchmark no query had all models wrong. Wavering Oracles, arXiv:2609.11428: best single 95.3%, oracle ceiling 99.8%, mean pairwise error correlation 0.285, effective number of independent models about 2.6 of 7. Wisdom and Delusion of LLM Ensembles for Code Generation and Repair, arXiv:2510.21513: ceiling about 83% above the best single model, with consensus selection falling into a popularity trap while a diversity-based strategy recovers up to 95% of the potential. DomainEval, arXiv:2408.13204: Pass@k above 75% in the computation domain versus 33.08% and 37.50% Pass@1 in cryptography and systems, with all models showing similar domain biases.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Not addressed.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Quantifies it as error correlation, which is the right currency: 7 participants with mean pairwise error correlation 0.285 behave like about 2.6 independent ones.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Two numbers should govern CDSFL's expectations. The effective-independence figure (about 2.6 of 7) says a 5-seat or 6-seat panel is not 5 or 6 independent falsifiers, and a 700-model roster is not 700 — consistent with the diversity-saturation result that fewer than 10 well-chosen agents capture most available diversity. The DomainEval finding is the sharpest constraint on the positional hypothesis: all models showed SIMILAR domain biases, a common trend of strengths and weaknesses. If every participant is weak on the same domains, routing cannot rescue those domains, and the positional gain is confined to the pairs where exactly one participant is right. That quantity is bounded by min(q, 1-p) for 2 participants with accuracies p and q (arXiv:2607.17384).

mechanisms.name: Heterogeneity-aware team selection: the realised gain is 0.80 percentage points
mechanisms.what_it_does: Scores each candidate by development-set accuracy plus 2 heterogeneity terms — error decorrelation via Yule's Q on pairwise correctness tables, and distributional divergence via Jensen-Shannon divergence over answer-option log-probabilities — then selects teams by multi-start greedy search on a standardised combined score (heterogeneity weights 0.13 and 0.05).
mechanisms.citation: Liangyu Teng et al., "Which Models Work Well Together? Measuring Heterogeneity for LLM Team Selection", arXiv:2609.38274 (29 Sep 2026)
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Requires a development-set accuracy per model per task, so it presupposes the probe. Its contribution is what to do with the probe results.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: This is the only paper found that selects a TEAM by measured heterogeneity rather than ranking individuals, which is the closest published analogue of CDSFL seating a panel.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: Directly applicable as the selection rule CDSFL actually needs, and simultaneously the most sobering number in this report. Selecting for heterogeneity beat selecting for quality alone by 0.80 percentage points (95% CI 0.44 to 1.16) on 7 primary benchmarks, 75.52% versus 74.72%, and by 0.31 points on 6 held-out benchmarks. It beat random selection by 3.58 points. The selected teams were IDENTICAL to quality-only selection on 4 of 7 benchmarks. So the full machinery of measured complementarity bought under 1 percentage point over just picking the best participants, and most of the apparent benefit of clever selection is the benefit of not selecting at random. The heterogeneity weights, 0.13 and 0.05, say the same thing: quality dominates.

mechanisms.name: Self-consistency and the non-monotonicity of adding calls
mechanisms.what_it_does: Samples several reasoning paths and takes the most frequent answer. A follow-up derives an analytical scaling model for voting systems and shows performance is not monotone in the number of calls.
mechanisms.citation: Xuezhi Wang et al., "Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models", arXiv:2203.11171, ICLR 2023: +17.9 points on GSM8K, +11.0 SVAMP, +12.2 AQuA, +6.4 StrategyQA, +3.9 ARC-challenge. Lingjiao Chen, Jared Quincy Davis, Boris Hanin, Peter Bailis, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, James Zou, "Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards the Scaling Properties of Compound AI Systems", arXiv:2403.02419, NeurIPS 2024.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Needs no capability model at all, which makes it the cheapest baseline a cold-start router must beat.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Self-consistency uses 1 participant many times, so it is the homogeneous baseline against which heterogeneous panels must justify themselves.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: The non-monotonicity result is the one to act on: voting performance first increases but then DECREASES as a function of the number of calls, because more calls help on queries the participant usually gets right and hurt on queries it usually gets wrong, and a task containing both produces a non-monotone curve. CDSFL's round counts and panel sizes are therefore not safely increasable, and the paper's contribution is that the optimum can be computed from a small number of samples. That is a concrete, cheap addition: fit the scaling model and set round count from it rather than by hand.

mechanisms.name: Multi-agent debate does not beat majority voting at equal cost
mechanisms.what_it_does: Compares multi-agent debate against a plain majority vote over independent samples at matched call budgets, and models debate as a martingale so that debate does not systematically improve or degrade beliefs on average.
mechanisms.citation: Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models?, arXiv:2508.17536, NeurIPS 2025: across 7 benchmarks majority voting without any debate performs on par with multi-agent debate in most cases. Jie Huang et al., "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet", arXiv:2310.01798, ICLR 2024: at an equal number of responses, multi-agent debate significantly underperforms simple self-consistency with majority voting. Qineng Wang et al., "Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?", ACL 2024 (aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.331): single-agent average 75.63 versus 70.04 for 3-agent debate, but multi-agent frameworks outperform single-agent when no demonstrations are provided.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_cold_start: Debate needs no capability estimates, so it is the other baseline a router must beat.
mechanisms.how_it_handles_heterogeneity: Mixture-of-Agents (Junlin Wang et al., arXiv:2406.04692, ICLR 2025) is the counterweight: 6 open proposers over 3 layers reached 65.1% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 against 57.5% for the strongest single model, and the authors report models write better answers when they can see other models' outputs even if those outputs are subpar.
mechanisms.transfers_to_cdsfl: This bears on CDSFL's architecture rather than its routing, but it bears hard. If debate's gains come mostly from aggregation rather than from participants changing each other's minds, then CDSFL's multi-round confer structure is paying round costs for a benefit a single-round vote would deliver. The conformity finding sharpens it: weak participants corrected only 3.6% of stance biases during debates, tending to abandon correct judgments and conform to the majority — which is a mechanism by which adding weak seats to a panel makes it worse, not just no better. The honest caveat is that debate DID consistently beat the single-agent baseline, and beat single-agent setups when no demonstrations were provided; the claim is only that it does not beat an equal-cost vote.

is_the_wheel_already_invented:
Largely yes, and in three separate places at once. The founder has independently arrived at three mechanisms that each have a named published form with optimality results he does not have.

Mechanism 1, the probe-then-tier cold start, is UniRoute (arXiv:2502.08773): represent every participant as a vector of error rates on representative prompt clusters, route by lowest cost-adjusted cluster error, admit participants never seen in training without retraining, with an excess risk bound and experiments over 30+ unseen models. The sparse-matrix version is EmbedLLM (ICLR 2025, arXiv:2410.02223), which does not require every participant to attempt every probe. The hybrid offline-online version is OrcaRouter (arXiv:2605.30736), which evaluates each candidate on a curated probe set to build a reward matrix and then keeps learning from live feedback.

Mechanism 1's recursion into easier problems for weaker participants is computerised adaptive testing under item response theory, which predates this entire literature. tinyBenchmarks (ICML 2024) estimates ability from 100 items within about 2% error where the full benchmark has 14,000. ATLAS (arXiv:2511.04689) matches whole-bank ability from 41 of 5,600 items by Fisher-information item selection, a 90% reduction. Fluid Benchmarking (arXiv:2509.11106) reports higher validity with 50 times fewer items. The published rule for choosing the next problem is information-maximising, not the founder's heuristic descent.

Mechanism 2, the no-prior knockout tournament, is dueling bandits. The cost-aware version is arXiv:2609.30360 (NeurIPS 2026): pairwise comparisons only, heterogeneous per-arm query costs, Track-and-Stop best-arm identification at prescribed confidence, proven asymptotically cost-optimal. The published finding that matters is older: AAAI-22's dueling-bandit approach to top-rating identification shows that random and round-robin pairing are the sample-INEFFICIENT baselines, beaten by upper-confidence-bound pair selection on a maintained candidate set.

What is NOT already invented: nobody in this literature routes among participants for FALSIFICATION work specifically, where the quantity being routed is a claim and the output is an attempted refutation rather than an answer. And the decentralised, server-free requirement is absent from all of it — the routing survey arXiv:2502.00409 names its open problems as standardising experiments, non-financial costs and adaptive strategies, and does not mention decentralised routing at all. Peer-to-peer model serving exists (Petals, petals.dev, routes requests through a chain of peers chosen to minimise total forward-pass time), but it distributes LAYERS of one model, not CLAIMS across many models, and a 2026 analysis (arXiv:2603.28622) notes such systems rely on greedy latency heuristics that assume cooperative peers.
strongest_disagreement:
The literature contradicts the founder's approach in four specific, citable places.

First and most directly, the knockout bracket is the wrong tournament and the published evidence says so twice over. Single elimination requires transitive preferences; the measured pairwise transitivity inconsistency for a strong judge is 15.22% of comparisons (TrustJudge, arXiv:2509.21117), and the ICML 2025 spotlight on non-transitivity (arXiv:2502.14074) shows rankings built from comparison against a fixed opponent are sensitive to the choice of that opponent, recommending full round-robin plus Bradley-Terry instead. Separately, sequential Elo from a single match ordering is unstable: scores can fluctuate dramatically based solely on the arbitrary ordering of matches when win probabilities approach 0.5, and stabilise only with 100 or more permutations (Boubdir et al., arXiv:2311.17295, GEM 2023, NeurIPS 2024 poster). A bracket is one ordering. And random pairing — "names drawn from a bag" — is the measured inefficient baseline, beaten by upper-confidence-bound pair selection (AAAI-22). Worst, single elimination removes a participant on one result, which contradicts the founder's own hard constraint that no model is ever permanently set aside.

Second, the recursive tier ladder will not pay for itself below tier 2. Across 5 benchmarks, 9 deferral scores and a pool of 8 models, allowing more than 2 models in a cascade did not improve mean test accuracy in 118 of 135 comparisons, adding at most 0.43 percentage points (arXiv:2605.06350). Deeper cascades helped only when the confidence score discriminated the current model's correct from incorrect answers, and the gain VANISHED when the score instead reflected query difficulty shared across models, at the same AUROC. A falsification harness's natural routing signal — claim hardness — is the shared-difficulty kind that was measured to kill the benefit.

Third, the single-ranked-roster output does not exist as a well-defined object. Model rankings reverse across token budgets on all benchmarks tested (p < 0.01, McNemar), over 4 models, 3 benchmarks, 56,476 inferences (arXiv:2608.12150). The founder's composite criterion — solved fastest, with tools, with proofs and falsifiers, most cost-effectively — silently fixes a budget and so produces one of several incompatible orderings, not the ordering. The same paper shows a domain-shaped router trained in one domain LOST 1.2 points when transferred to another while gaining 1.6 to 5.7 within domain, which is the positional hypothesis failing exactly where he wants to use it.

Fourth, the strong form of the positional hypothesis is contradicted by the largest factor analysis available: 156 models, 10 benchmarks, parallel analysis indicating a single-factor solution accounting for 75% of total variance (arXiv:2603.02540). A football-position analogy needs positions to be substantially orthogonal; 75% shared variance says they are mostly one axis. The corroborating practical number is that selecting a team by measured error-decorrelation and distributional divergence beat selecting on quality alone by 0.80 percentage points (95% CI 0.44 to 1.16), with the selected teams IDENTICAL to quality-only on 4 of 7 benchmarks (arXiv:2609.38274). The weak form survives and is well supported — equal-scoring participants disagree on 16% to 38% of items even at the frontier (arXiv:2602.11898), and 2 models 6 arena points apart have visibly different 8-factor skill profiles (arXiv:2507.20208) — but the measured gain from exploiting it has so far been under 1 percentage point, against an oracle ceiling of 12.0 to 27.8 points. The gap between ceiling and realised gain is the thing to be sceptical about, not the ceiling.

One further contradiction that cuts at the foundation: both mechanisms need a judge, and panel judging re-admits vendor identity through the back door. In a fully crossed design over 4 model families with 9,312 judgments, every family showed a same-family preference lift of 3.4 to 8.4 percentage points, the global family-preference statistic was 0.067 (95% CI 0.053 to 0.084, permutation p = 0.0002), 55.4% of AB/BA pairs reversed under order swap, and panel composition changed 18.5% of pairwise outcomes relative to a family-balanced reference (arXiv:2609.17857). A tournament in which the participants judge each other does not measure capability alone; it measures capability plus who is seated.
open_problems: Decentralised routing. No paper found addresses routing among models with no central server. Every method surveyed assumes a central router holding the capability estimates. The routing survey (arXiv:2502.00409) names its open problems as standardising experiments, non-financial costs and adaptive strategies, and does not mention decentralisation. Peer-to-peer model serving (Petals) distributes layers of one model, not claims across many models, and a 2026 analysis (arXiv:2603.28622) observes such systems optimise throughput and connectivity rather than execution trust, relying on greedy latency heuristics that assume cooperative peers.

Roster-scale evidence. The largest unseen-model routing experiment found covers more than 30 models (UniRoute, arXiv:2502.08773); the largest heterogeneity-team-selection study uses 7 primary benchmarks and a modest pool; RouterBench uses 11 models. Nothing found tests 70 or 700 participants. The diversity-saturation result (fewer than 10 well-chosen agents capture most available diversity, arXiv:2607.09197) suggests the large-roster case may be uninteresting rather than unsolved, but that has not been measured at 700.

Calibrating an uncalibrated item bank. Adaptive testing needs item difficulty and discrimination estimated from prior test-takers. The founder's randomly generated problems have neither. No method found generates probe items with analytically known difficulty parameters, and ATLAS (arXiv:2511.04689) reports 3% to 6% of items in a mature bank have negative discrimination, so a generator will produce broken probes with no published discard rule.

Routing for falsification rather than answering. The entire literature routes a QUERY to a model that will answer it. Nothing found routes a CLAIM to a participant likeliest to refute it. Whether a model's refutation capability is correlated with its answering capability is unmeasured, and the proof-grading results (up to 65.5% accuracy collapse under step-wise scrutiny, arXiv:2506.07927) suggest they may diverge sharply.

Reference-free grading of reasoning. Reference-based judging closes the cheap-judge versus frontier-judge gap entirely, while reference-free leaves about 10%. CDSFL's live falsification work has no reference by construction, and no published method grades novel proofs reliably without one.

Capability drift over time. Contamination studies (GSM1k, arXiv:2405.00332) measure drift between a public benchmark and a fresh set at one moment. Nothing found measures how fast a measured capability estimate decays, so there is no published answer to how often a cold-start probe must be re-run.

Exploration floors that respect a no-retirement constraint. The collapse results (LinUCB collapsing to a single arm, arXiv:2510.02850; routing collapse, arXiv:2602.03478) establish the failure mode and name Thompson sampling and rank-learning as fixes, but no paper found states a minimum per-participant traffic share that guarantees capability estimates stay current for every participant.

Whether the first factor of a FALSIFICATION outcome matrix carries 75% of variance like the general-benchmark one does, or splits into skills like the 44-benchmark one. This is the single measurement that would settle the positional question for CDSFL, and it is a measurement CDSFL can make on its own data and nobody else has made.
